paragraphs: The paper asks how widely a familiar method for finding network communities can be trusted. Earlier theory had established strong recovery results for the Stochastic Block Model and its degree-corrected extension. These models describe networks with community structure, but guarantees for them leave open whether the same algorithm works for a broader range of network models.

The authors introduce Preference Frame Models, a wider class of block models, and show that essentially the same spectral clustering algorithm applies. The algorithm uses the graph's normalized Laplacian to extract information about its community structure. Within the proposed model class, it retains essentially the same high-probability, nearly perfect recovery guarantees associated with the earlier models.

A second contribution is the way the model class is described mathematically. Its parametrization makes the available degrees of freedom explicit, and the recovery bounds clarify which parameters govern error. The result therefore extends the reach of an existing algorithm while making its theoretical behavior easier to interpret within this broader class.
neurips-2015-a-class-of-network-models-r.tldr: Preference Frame Models broaden the network models for which familiar spectral clustering methods have strong community-recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Online learning studies decisions made as data arrive, with performance assessed through regret. This paper asks when regret guarantees can adapt to the particular data or model involved. Rather than studying each proposed guarantee separately, it develops a framework for deciding whether an algorithm can achieve a desired adaptive bound.

The approach modifies sequential complexity measures, which capture the difficulty of learning across a sequence of decisions. Each candidate adaptive rate produces a collection of offset complexity measures. Proving sufficiently small upper bounds on these quantities is enough to establish that the rate is achievable. The analysis uses one-sided tail inequalities to control the relevant random processes.

This framework recovers and improves several kinds of existing adaptive guarantees, including quantile, second-order, and small-loss bounds. It also yields a spectral-norm-based bound for online linear optimization and a new online PAC-Bayes theorem. The main value is a shared method for establishing achievability across different forms of adaptation; the stated conditions are sufficient, rather than a claim that every achievable bound must satisfy them.
neurips-2015-adaptive-online-learning-5b.tldr: A unified complexity-based framework gives sufficient conditions for achieving regret bounds that adapt to online learning data and models.

paragraphs: When measurements must be stored using a fixed number of bits, there is a choice between collecting more coarse measurements and fewer precise ones. This paper studies that choice for sparse signal recovery from linear measurements. Each of the m measurements receives b bits, so the total budget is B = m × b.

The authors propose b-bit Marginal Regression and derive a single expression that characterizes the trade-off between measurement count and precision. For estimating the signal's direction, represented by its unit vector, one bit per measurement is optimal in the setting they analyze. This result covers any level of additive Gaussian noise before quantization, as well as adversarial noise.

The distinction between direction and magnitude matters. The one-bit conclusion concerns the unit vector, rather than full recovery of the signal's scale. For two or more bits per measurement, the paper establishes optimality of Lloyd-Max quantization and shows that maximum likelihood can consistently estimate the signal's norm. Together, these results connect allocation of a bit budget to the particular aspect of the signal being estimated.
neurips-2015-b-bit-marginal-regression-d.tldr: Under a fixed bit budget, one-bit measurements are optimal for estimating sparse signal direction in the analyzed setting.

paragraphs: This paper connects two capabilities that do not naturally fit together: training neural networks with backpropagation and running them on energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Backpropagation works with continuous quantities, whereas the hardware uses spikes and discrete synapses. That mismatch makes it difficult to transfer a conventionally trained network directly into the hardware's operating format.

The authors represent spikes and discrete synapses through continuous probabilities during training. This makes standard backpropagation available without requiring the deployed network to use continuous outputs or weights. After training, they sample those probabilities to produce one or more hardware-compatible networks. When multiple networks are produced, ensemble averaging combines their outputs.

A sparsely connected network on the TrueNorth chip demonstrates the approach using MNIST. An ensemble of 64 reaches 99.42% accuracy while consuming 121 microjoules per image. A single-network configuration reaches 92.7% at 0.408 microjoules per image. These two reported configurations illustrate a practical accuracy–energy trade-off: the probabilistic training method supports both a higher-performing ensemble and a much lower-energy individual network.
neurips-2015-backpropagation-for-energy-.tldr: Training with continuous probabilities lets backpropagation produce spiking networks that trade accuracy against energy use on neuromorphic hardware.

paragraphs: Estimating generalized linear models in high dimensions can call for computationally complex regularized maximum-likelihood procedures. This paper develops a simpler alternative: estimators that can be expressed in closed form. The goal is to retain strong statistical behavior while reducing the computational work needed to obtain parameter estimates and identify relevant variables.

The construction begins with modified versions of the ordinary, unregularized maximum-likelihood estimator. These variants are designed to remain well-defined in high-dimensional settings and to have explicit formulas. Thresholding operations then turn them into the proposed estimator family. This separates the initial calculation from the operation that selects which estimated effects to retain.

A unified analysis provides guarantees for both parameter estimation error and variable selection that match those of the more complex regularized GLM estimators considered. The authors work out specific versions for logistic, exponential, and Poisson regression, and support the statistical and computational findings with extensive simulations. The contribution is a common construction showing that simpler computation can preserve strong guarantees across these models.
neurips-2015-closed-form-estimators-for-.tldr: Closed-form, thresholded GLM estimators match strong guarantees of more complex regularized estimators while simplifying computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions in which success requires every selected component to work, but feedback reveals only the first failure. Network routing provides an example: a chosen path succeeds only if all its links are available, and a blocked path may reveal only its first unavailable link. Learning must proceed from this incomplete information.

The proposed combinatorial cascading bandit model lets an agent choose a constrained, ordered collection of items. Item weights are independent stochastic binary variables, and reward is received exactly when all selected weights equal one. The authors introduce CombCascade, an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds, and prove both gap-dependent and gap-free bounds on regret over n steps.

The analysis handles two intertwined difficulties: the reward depends nonlinearly on all selected items, and observations stop at the first failure. Evaluations on two real-world problems show good performance even when the modeling assumptions are violated. Those experiments provide evidence beyond the theoretical setting, while the formal guarantees belong to the stated model. The paper also demonstrates why this feedback structure requires a new learning algorithm.
neurips-2015-combinatorial-cascading-ban.tldr: CombCascade learns constrained combinations from first-failure feedback, with regret guarantees for independent binary item outcomes.

paragraphs: Standard decision-tree training chooses splits one node at a time. Each choice is judged locally, even though the usefulness of a split also depends on the rest of the tree. This paper addresses the resulting possibility of suboptimal trees by optimizing split functions throughout the tree together with the parameters at its leaves.

The authors connect learning oblique splits, which use linear combinations of input features, to structured prediction with latent variables. They derive a convex-concave upper bound on the tree's empirical loss and optimize this surrogate global objective. Joint optimization lets training account for how decisions at different levels contribute to the same overall prediction task.

The gradient calculation for each training example costs O(d²), where d is tree depth, making training deep trees feasible. Stochastic gradient descent supports training on large datasets. Across several classification benchmarks, the resulting trees outperform the greedy decision-tree baselines evaluated. These findings support the practical value of coordinating splits across levels, without asserting that the optimization always finds the globally best tree.
neurips-2015-efficient-non-greedy-optimi.tldr: Jointly optimizing tree splits and leaf parameters produces decision trees that outperform greedy baselines on the evaluated classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: A series of photographs often records a shared experience, so describing each image in isolation can miss relationships across the collection. This paper tackles the generation of a sequence of sentences from a sequence of images. It extends image description from individual image–sentence pairs to a setting where the surrounding sequence also matters.

The proposed coherent recurrent convolutional network combines convolutional networks, bidirectional recurrent networks, and an entity-based local coherence model. These components bring visual processing, sequence context, and coherence between nearby descriptions into one architecture. The model learns directly from user-generated blog posts, using their text and images as paired training material.

The authors evaluate the approach with quantitative measures, including BLEU and top-K recall, and with human judgments collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk. They report that it outperforms the other state-of-the-art candidate methods considered. The findings support treating an image stream as a connected description task: the system is designed to produce sentences that account for a collection, rather than merely assembling independently generated captions.
neurips-2015-expressing-an-image-stream-.tldr: A network trained on illustrated blog posts generates sentence sequences for image streams using visual context and local coherence.

paragraphs: This paper compares ways to classify data when each of two classes has a multivariate Gaussian feature distribution and both classes share the same covariance matrix. In this setting, Bayes' rule gives a linear classifier associated with Linear Discriminant Analysis. However, the usual generative estimation approach can behave poorly when the number of features is large.

The authors develop an analysis of classification error that applies to any linear discriminant approach under these Gaussian models. This provides a common basis for comparing generative estimation, methods that learn the discriminant function directly, and logistic regression. The comparison focuses on prediction error rather than simply how accurately each method estimates distributional parameters.

Under the stated sparsity assumption, ℓ1-regularized logistic regression achieves a rate of O(s log p / n), where s is the sparsity of the Bayes classifier, p the feature count, and n the sample count. The compared alternatives are either inconsistent in high dimensions or have the slower square-root rate. The advantage is established within this shared-covariance Gaussian and sparse-classifier setting.
neurips-2015-fast-classification-rates-f.tldr: Under sparse, shared-covariance Gaussian class models, ℓ1-regularized logistic regression achieves faster classification rates than the compared approaches.

paragraphs: Object detection systems need candidate regions indicating where objects might be. As detection networks became faster, generating those proposals emerged as a major remaining computational cost. Faster R-CNN addresses that bottleneck by making proposal generation a neural-network component that shares image features with the detector.

The Region Proposal Network is fully convolutional and predicts both object boundaries and objectness scores at each position. It is trained end to end to produce proposals that Fast R-CNN then uses for detection. A simple alternating optimization procedure trains the two networks to share convolutional features, allowing proposal generation to reuse computation already needed for detecting objects.

With the very deep VGG-16 model, the complete system runs at five frames per second on a GPU, including all processing steps. Using 300 proposals per image, it reports 73.2% mean average precision on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 70.4% on 2012, described as state-of-the-art accuracy. The contribution is the combination of effective detection and nearly cost-free proposals through shared full-image features.
neurips-2015-faster-r-cnn-towards-real-t.tldr: Faster R-CNN shares convolutional features between region proposal and detection networks to reduce proposal cost while maintaining strong detection accuracy.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models require learning from data when some relevant variables are unobserved. This paper develops a general theory for expectation-maximization in high-dimensional versions of these models. It addresses both obtaining accurate parameter estimates and using those estimates to test hypotheses about selected components of the parameter.

For estimation, the authors propose an EM algorithm that incorporates sparsity into the learning process. With an appropriate initialization, it converges geometrically and reaches an estimator with a near-optimal or optimal statistical convergence rate. These are distinct benefits: geometric convergence concerns progress across algorithmic iterations, while the statistical rate describes the accuracy attainable from the data.

The second contribution builds an inferential procedure on the resulting estimator. It supports hypothesis tests for low-dimensional parts of a parameter that is high-dimensional overall. For a broad family of statistical models, the authors present the framework as the first computationally feasible route to optimal estimation and asymptotic inference in high dimensions. The initialization requirement is central to the stated convergence guarantee.
neurips-2015-high-dimensional-em-algorit.tldr: A sparsity-aware EM framework combines fast convergence from appropriate initialization with strong estimation guarantees and asymptotic hypothesis testing.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common backpropagation framework for learning policies that choose continuous actions. A central challenge is incorporating randomness into the calculation of how policy changes affect future value. The authors handle this by expressing stochasticity in the Bellman equation as a deterministic function of external noise.

That representation produces a family of policy-gradient algorithms spanning different uses of learned models and value functions. At one end are model-free methods with value functions; at the other are model-based methods without them. Although the framework uses learned models, it requires observations from the environment rather than observations along trajectories predicted by those models, reducing the impact of model errors accumulating across simulated steps.

The algorithms are evaluated on a toy stochastic control problem and several physics-based control problems in simulation. One variant, SVG(1), demonstrates the effectiveness of learning a model, value function, and policy simultaneously in continuous domains. The contribution is both a unifying way to derive these algorithms and evidence that the combined learning strategy can work in the simulated tasks considered.
neurips-2015-learning-continuous-control.tldr: Stochastic value gradients unify continuous-control policy learning through backpropagation while reducing reliance on model-predicted trajectories.

paragraphs: Repeated measurements can reveal how individuals or objects change, but their trajectories may differ in both direction and speed. This paper introduces a Bayesian mixed-effects model that estimates a typical group trajectory while allowing individual variations. It focuses on measurements with smooth constraints, represented as points on a Riemannian manifold.

Individual trajectories arise through spatiotemporal transformations of the group-average trajectory. These transformations can change where a trajectory goes and how quickly it is followed. Riemannian geometry provides a common mathematical framework for respecting the measurement constraints, and stochastic approximations of expectation-maximization estimate the parameters in this highly nonlinear model.

The authors apply the method to cognitive changes during the onset of Alzheimer's disease. Their experimental results show correspondence between individuals' diagnosis ages, supporting the interpretation that the model learned a normative progression scenario. The random effects also reveal differences in the ordering and timing of cognitive impairments. The result is a way to describe shared progression together with variation across individuals, rather than reducing all longitudinal change to a single common pace.
neurips-2015-learning-spatiotemporal-tra.tldr: A Bayesian manifold model learns a shared trajectory of change alongside individual differences in its direction and timing.

paragraphs: Training for multiple passes over a dataset changes both the optimization process and the resulting predictor. This paper studies that connection for least-squares learning with an incremental gradient method. Its central question is how the number of epochs can control learning when the other algorithm parameters have already been fixed.

The authors show that the epoch count acts as a regularization parameter in their method. This gives the decision about how long to train a statistical role, alongside its obvious computational role. The analysis connects the algorithm's successive iterates to their prediction risk, bringing optimization behavior and statistical learning guarantees into the same argument.

The paper proves strong universal consistency, expressed as almost-sure convergence of the risk, and derives sharp finite-sample bounds for the iterates. The first result concerns eventual statistical behavior, while the second addresses accuracy with a finite amount of data. Together, they provide a theoretical step toward understanding multiple epochs in stochastic gradient techniques, specifically through the incremental least-squares regularization algorithm studied here.
neurips-2015-learning-with-incremental-i.tldr: For incremental least-squares learning with other parameters fixed, the number of epochs serves as regularization with consistency and finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Variational inference uses an adjustable probability distribution to approximate a distribution of interest. Stochastic optimization can update that approximation using sampled gradients, but noisy estimates complicate the updates. This paper introduces local expectation gradients, a general-purpose method that organizes gradient estimation around the particular variational parameter being updated.

The method divides a gradient-estimation problem involving many parameters into smaller tasks. For each task, it computes an exact expectation over the single random variable most correlated with the parameter of interest. Sampling still supplies information from the variational distribution, while this targeted averaging produces a Rao-Blackwellized estimate with low variance.

The approach works efficiently with both continuous and discrete random variables, giving it scope across different kinds of probabilistic models. Its local computations resemble aspects of Gibbs sampling, but the proposed algorithm can also be straightforwardly parallelized. The significance is the combination of focused exact averaging and stochastic estimation: each subtask spends computation on the part of the distribution most relevant to its parameter, while remaining suitable for parallel execution.
neurips-2015-local-expectation-gradients.tldr: Local expectation gradients use targeted exact averaging to obtain low-variance, parallelizable stochastic gradients for variational inference.

paragraphs: Maximum-likelihood learning becomes difficult when an undirected graphical model makes inference computationally intractable. A common response is to restrict the model to tree-structured parameters. This paper explores another restriction: allow parameters only in a set where Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling is guaranteed to converge quickly to its stationary distribution.

For exponential families with bounded sufficient statistics, the authors prove that gradient descent using sampling-based gradient estimates can approximate the best likelihood solution within such a fast-mixing set, with high probability. The result extends beyond graphical models. Its target is explicitly the optimum inside the constrained set, making the parameter restriction part of the guarantee.

Without regularization, obtaining error ε in log-likelihood takes effort cubic in 1/ε, apart from logarithmic factors. With ridge regularization, strong convexity gives quadratic dependence for error ε in parameter distance. These are different accuracy criteria, so the rates should be read accordingly. Both results provide fully polynomial-time randomized approximation schemes, giving theoretical support to sampled-gradient learning under the stated restrictions.
neurips-2015-maximum-likelihood-learning.tldr: Restricting parameters to fast-mixing sets gives high-probability approximation guarantees for maximum-likelihood learning with sampled gradients.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test a structural claim about an unknown probability distribution from samples. The goal is to distinguish distributions belonging to a specified family from distributions far from every member of that family. The families considered include monotone, log-concave, unimodal, and monotone-hazard-rate distributions.

The authors develop a general approach that yields computationally efficient testers with optimal sample requirements for all these families. A central component compares an unknown distribution with a known candidate: it distinguishes closeness in chi-squared distance from being far apart in total variation distance. The use of two different distance notions is part of the testing problem solved by this component.

Matching lower bounds establish that the sample requirements cannot be improved for the tested problems. The construction also produces computationally efficient proper learners for discrete log-concave and monotone-hazard-rate distributions, meaning that their learned distributions belong to the target family. Experiments illustrate the testers' effectiveness. The work thus combines optimal testing guarantees with learning procedures needed to make those tests computationally practical.
neurips-2015-optimal-testing-for-propert.tldr: A general testing approach achieves optimal sample complexity and efficient computation for several structured distribution families.

paragraphs: High-dimensional observations may lie near a smooth structure with far fewer dimensions. Many manifold-learning methods map observations onto such a structure, but this paper seeks a probabilistic model that learns both the structure and the distribution generating the observations. It identifies identifiability problems in Gaussian process latent variable models as an obstacle to that goal.

The authors introduce a Coulomb repulsive process for the locations of points on the manifold, inspired by electrostatic interactions between particles. They combine this process with a Gaussian process prior for the function mapping those locations into the observation space. The resulting electrostatic Gaussian process couples the arrangement of latent points with a probabilistic mapping to observed data.

The paper focuses on one-dimensional manifolds, or curves, and develops efficient inference algorithms for this case. Experiments show substantially improved performance across several tasks, including filling in missing video frames. The contribution is a probabilistic curve-learning construction that addresses the identified ambiguities in latent locations, with practical evidence from the one-dimensional setting studied.
neurips-2015-probabilistic-curve-learnin.tldr: An electrostatic Gaussian process combines repulsive latent locations with a probabilistic mapping to improve learning of one-dimensional manifolds.

paragraphs: Approximate singular value decomposition seeks a compact, low-rank representation of a matrix. Randomized simultaneous power iteration provides strong approximation accuracy without relying on gaps between singular values. This paper improves its iteration requirement while retaining that independence from singular-value gaps, which the authors describe as unreliable in practice.

The proposed randomized block Krylov method is closely related to Block Lanczos. It reaches a low-rank approximation within a factor of 1 + ε of optimal spectral-norm error in roughly O(1/√ε) iterations, compared with roughly O(1/ε) for simultaneous iteration. The paper proves the improvement and reports substantially better experimental performance.

The authors also separate low-rank approximation quality from principal-component quality. A strong spectral-norm error guarantee alone does not establish that the returned principal components are good. They prove that both block Krylov iteration and simultaneous iteration provide nearly optimal PCA for any matrix. This additional result addresses a distinct requirement of data analysis and strengthens the justification for using these iterative methods over non-iterative sketching approaches.
neurips-2015-randomized-block-krylov-met.tldr: Randomized block Krylov iteration accelerates approximate SVD guarantees without singular-value-gap assumptions and also provides nearly optimal PCA.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when some response values have been deliberately corrupted. The adversary may choose both the affected responses and their corrupted values after seeing the data matrix and underlying model. This is a stronger corruption setting than one that requires the errors to be chosen independently of the inputs.

The authors propose TORRENT, a simple hard-thresholding algorithm. Under stated deterministic conditions on the data matrix, it exactly recovers the underlying parameter despite adversarial response corruption. The abstract states that these conditions are satisfied by sub-Gaussian sampling. The recovery results are universal over the underlying parameter, rather than applying only to a fixed parameter selected independently of the matrix.

Gradient-descent-based extensions aim to handle larger problems, including high-dimensional sparse recovery, and receive similar recovery guarantees. Experiments report significantly faster recovery than leading ℓ1 solvers. In one example with 50,000 features and around 40% corrupted responses, TORRENT-HYB is more than twenty times faster than the best compared ℓ1 solver. This measured speed advantage complements the conditional exact-recovery theory.
neurips-2015-robust-regression-via-hard-.tldr: TORRENT uses hard thresholding to recover linear models under adversarial response corruption, with conditional guarantees and strong empirical speedups.

paragraphs: Submodular and supermodular functions capture ideas such as diversity and regularity. Although they are often studied as optimization objectives, they can also define probability distributions. This paper examines that probabilistic use, where inference can describe predictive uncertainty rather than only return an optimized solution.

The authors study Markov chain Monte Carlo inference for general log-submodular and log-supermodular models, a class extending beyond familiar examples such as Ising models and determinantal point processes. They focus on a simple Gibbs sampler and establish two sufficient conditions for its convergence behavior. One guarantees polynomial-time mixing; the other guarantees the faster O(n log n) mixing rate.

Mixing guarantees explain how quickly sampling approaches the model's target distribution, which matters when samples are used for approximate marginal inference. The conditions therefore identify cases where this straightforward sampler has a computational guarantee, without claiming that all models in the class mix quickly. The authors also evaluate the sampler on three example models and compare it with a recently proposed variational approach.
neurips-2015-sampling-from-probabilistic.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for efficient Gibbs sampling in general log-submodular and log-supermodular probabilistic models.

paragraphs: This paper studies graph transduction using embeddings that place graph vertices on a unit sphere. It establishes that orthonormal representations, a class of these embeddings, are PAC learnable. Because the relevant function class has infinite VC dimension, the authors derive a different generalization bound connected to the Lovász theta function.

That bound motivates SPORE, a spectral-regularized orthonormal embedding objective. The objective is convex but nonsmooth and is optimized over an elliptope. Standard semidefinite programming approaches to such problems have O(n⁶) time complexity, making the computation itself an important obstacle to applying the theoretical construction to larger graphs.

The proposed Infeasible Inexact Proximal method uses approximate projections that need not be feasible, and achieves O(1/√T) convergence. For SPORE, FISTA computes the approximate projection step. The authors report scaling to thousands of vertices, compared with only a few hundred for standard semidefinite programming. The optimization method applies more generally when a suitable approximate projection exists, and the learning analysis also extends to multiple graphs.
neurips-2015-spectral-norm-regularizatio.tldr: SPORE combines a graph-embedding generalization bound with approximate-projection optimization that scales beyond standard semidefinite programming.

paragraphs: A recommendation can depend on when it is made as well as on which item a user likes. This paper addresses two related questions: which item is desirable at a particular moment, and when a user will return to a service. Both require modeling recurring activity patterns rather than treating interactions as timeless preferences.

The proposed framework combines self-exciting point processes with low-rank models to capture temporal recurrence across user–item pairs. It connects the timing of activity with shared structure across a large collection of interactions. The authors show that model parameters can be estimated through convex optimization and develop an efficient algorithm with an O(1/ε) convergence rate.

The algorithm scales to millions of user–item pairs and billions of temporal events. Evaluations on synthetic and real datasets report strong predictive performance relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods on both timing-sensitive questions. The formulation can also incorporate profile, textual, and spatial information. Its contribution is a unified way to model what users consume and when their recurring activity is likely to occur.
neurips-2015-time-sensitive-recommendati.tldr: Combining temporal point processes with low-rank models improves prediction of timely recommendations and users' next return times.

paragraphs: Restricted Boltzmann machines are undirected neural networks used for unsupervised learning, including initialization of deeper networks. Their practical usefulness has depended partly on stochastic training procedures such as contrastive divergence. This paper develops a deterministic iterative alternative, changing how training is carried out while retaining the same model family.

The method uses the Thouless-Anderson-Palmer approach, an improved mean-field approximation from statistical physics. This supplies a basis for iterative training together with a clear objective function that is easy to evaluate. Having an accessible objective gives the procedure an explicit quantity through which its training behavior can be assessed.

The authors demonstrate performance equal to, and sometimes better than, persistent contrastive divergence. This supports deterministic mean-field training as a practical alternative in the evaluations reported. They also suggest that the strategy could extend to other models and to more accurate higher-order approximations. Those extensions are presented as a promising direction, with the demonstrated contribution being the proposed training procedure and its comparison with persistent contrastive divergence.
neurips-2015-training-restricted-boltzma.tldr: A deterministic TAP-based training procedure matches or sometimes exceeds persistent contrastive divergence while providing an easily evaluated objective.

paragraphs: Increasing neural-network depth can be valuable, but it also makes training more difficult. This paper introduces highway networks to address the difficulty of training very deep architectures. Its central design goal is to let information travel across many layers without being obstructed by the depth of the network.

Highway networks use adaptive gating units inspired by Long Short-Term Memory recurrent networks. These gates regulate information flow along pathways that the authors call information highways. The architecture therefore makes control over information passage part of the network itself, providing a way to support communication across a large number of layers during learning.

The authors report that highway networks with hundreds of layers can be trained directly using simple gradient descent. This establishes the trainability of extremely deep networks using the proposed architecture and opens them to further study. The finding concerns overcoming a training obstacle: it enables investigation of very deep, efficient architectures without implying that every additional layer necessarily improves performance on every task.
neurips-2015-training-very-deep-networks.tldr: Highway networks use adaptive gates to support information flow across hundreds of layers and enable direct training with gradient descent.
